data.title: The Oral GLP-1 Tracker: Foundayo surges as Wegovy pill stalls
data.description:
With the recent launches of Novo Nordisk’s Wegovy pill and Eli Lilly’s Foundayo, the obesity market has started to shift toward oral GLP-1 drugs. While Novo leverages its first-mover advantage with the familiar Wegovy brand, Lilly is betting that the freedom from strict fasting and water requirements can give Foundayo an edge.

Each week, Fierce Pharma’s Oral GLP-1 Tracker will leverage analysts’ notes and IQVIA data to monitor prescription trends and shifting market shares as these two titans vie to become the go-to oral weight-loss solution for millions.

UPDATED: Oct. 2, 2026

Eli Lilly's Foundayo is showing clearer signs of acceleration. Total prescriptions for the oral GLP-1 receptor agonist surged about 21% to 64,268 during last week, according to IQVIA data cited by Citi. That haul came off a 13% sequential increase the week before that.

"We're seeing early signs of growth in Q3 for Foundayo," Jefferies analysts wrote in an Oct. 2 note.

Recent expansion of Foundayo could be attributed to a direct-to-consumer ad first aired in late August featuring Martha Steward, as well as the Medicare GLP-1 Bridge program which, beginning in July, offers eligible seniors GLP-1 obesity drugs at a $50 monthly copay.

Meanwhile, Novo's Wegovy pill scripts appear stuck at just above $180K. Except for a Labor Day holiday lull, total weekly scripts for the oral semaglutide have hovered between 181K and 184K over the past five weeks, including 182K last week, according to Citi.

It's worth noting that Foundayo took 25 weeks to reach where Wegovy pill achieved in just seven weeks in terms of total scripts. But the gap between the two drugs are closing. As Jefferies noted, Lilly owned 26% of the oral obesity market as of last week, versus a little less than 23% in the previous two weeks.

Overall, Lilly's Zepbound remains the obesity market leader with total scripts of 805.7K, up 2.3% sequentially, according to Citi. Novo's total Wegovy scripts for both the pill and the injectable were down 0.6% sequentially to a 519.6K.

UPDATED: Sept. 25, 2026

Total prescriptions for both Eli Lilly's Foundayo and Novo's Wegovy pill have bounced back following a holiday dip and reached new records. Weekly scripts for the Wegov pill jumped 14% sequentially to about 184K, compared with its previous high of 183K, according to IQVIA data cited by Citi. Foundayo climbed 13% to cross 50K for the first time, reaching 53,321.

Foundayo now captures about 1 out of 3 new starts for oral GLP-1 obesity drugs, and “that’s growing week over week,” Lilly CEO David Ricks told CNBC in an interview this week. 

As Leerink Partners analysts noted in a Sept. 23 note, effective Sept. 1, Lilly cut the initial-dose pricing for Foundayo 0.8 mg, 2.5 mg and 5.5 mg to $149, $149 and $199 per month for self-pay patients, respectively. The company framed the promotion as an elasticity experiment and as a push to the first maintenance dose, according to the Leerink note.

As Jefferies analysts pointed out in a Sept. 25 note, the majority of Foundayo scripts seem to be cash pay, with about 80% of patients still on starting doses.

Based on the IQVIA data so far, the Jefferies team estimated U.S. Foundayo revenues of $203 million in the third quarter, slightly lower than the $209 million consensus projection. 

Broadly speaking, Lilly yielded 0.6 percentage point of its obesity market share to Novo during the previous week, but still maintained its share level above 60%, according to Citi. 

In the recently launched Medicare GLP-1 Bridge program, Lilly is capturing 7 out of 10 patients, with many on its Zepbound, Ricks told CNBC. Foundayo, according to Ricks, is attracting Medicare patients looking for convenience but not necessarily a huge weight-loss effect. 

UPDATED: Sept. 18, 2026

As expected, the past U.S. Labor Day holiday took a toll on obesity drugs' prescription numbers. According to IQVIA data cited by Citi, weekly scripts for Novo's Wegovy pill dropped roughly 12% sequentially to about 161K for the last week. The decline for Foundayo was modest, at just 1%, as the Lilly drug still managed to rake in more than 47K scripts. 

Lilly this week said Foundayo captured more than 30% of new patients in the U.S. market for oral obesity ​treatments, Reuters reported. 

Citing Bloomberg Symphony data, Jefferies analysts suggested in a Friday note that Foundayo's recent acceleration "has been driven primarily by retail/commercial channels."

Elsewhere, Lilly's total Zepbound scripts were down 8.5% week over week, but the GIP/GLP-1 drug expanded its market share by 0.4% versus Novo's Wegovy franchise, whose scripts decreased 10% during the period.

UPDATED: Sept. 11, 2026

Both Novo Nordisk’s Wegovy pill and Eli Lilly’s Foundayo saw their highest total prescriptions so far over the past week as the companies’ oral obesity battle continues to play out.  

According to IQVIA data cited by Citi, the Wegovy pill reached an approximate 183K total scripts for the most recent reporting period, versus 181K the week prior. Foundayo, for its part, climbed nearly 8% to reach 47.5K scripts. Citi analysts emphasized that IQVIA may still be missing some Foundayo prescriptions made through telehealth channels. 

Meanwhile, using the last four weeks as a guide, total GLP-1 prescriptions have increased by 5.4%, compared to a 6.8% decline the prior year, the Citi team said. Citi analysts attributed the 12-percentage-point swing to the expansion of oral GLP-1 therapies, which is likely broadening access to the class and drawing in new patients.  

Across the broader landscape, Lilly’s tirzepatide currently holds a nearly 57% share of the total GLP-1 market, compared to around 49.5% last year, while Novo’s semaglutide has stayed relatively flat at a 37% share, the analysts added.  

UPDATED: Sept. 4, 2026

Total prescriptions for Novo Nordisk's Wegovy pill and Eli Lilly's Foundayo both grew over the past week, reaching roughly 181K (+3%) and 44K (+8%), IQVIA data showed, as cited by Citi. Both numbers are the two meds' highest so far. 

While Foundayo has yet to catch up with the Wegovy pill, the market share gap between the two oral drugs is slowly narrowing. According to an Aug. 28 Jefferies note based on data the previous week, Foundayo's share of new prescriptions (NRx), which exclude refills, was 21.5% in the oral obesity market.

Back to the most recent week, the Wegovy pill's position within the Wegovy family remained stable at 35%, as total Wegovy scripts increased 2.7% sequentially to 513.5K. During the same period, Lilly's Zepbound scripts climbed 1.6% to a little fewer than 772K.  

UPDATE: Aug. 28, 2026

Twenty weeks into its launch, Eli Lilly's Foundayo has finally exceeded 40,000 in weekly prescriptions, according to IQVIA data cited by Citi. The oral GLP-1 drug posted 40,862 scripts last week, bouncing back from a small dip the week prior. Still, the drug's scripts level is no match for the roughly 57K that Novo Nordisk's Wegovy pill garnered at week 6 of its own launch.

In its 33rd week of launch, the Wegovy pill booked roughly 175K scripts, slightly down from 176K, per IQVIA. The share of the oral version of semaglutide in all Wegovy obesity scripts was flat week over week at 35%. All told, across the pill and the injectable, Wegovy's weekly scripts were a little over 500K, down 0.8% sequentially.

As Jefferies analysts observed in an Aug. 21 note, Wegovy has been relatively flat since the Medicare GLP-1 Bridge program began July 1.

Overall, the roughly 60%-40% obesity market share split between Lilly and Novo remained stable, as Lilly's Zepbound held its ground as the most popular drug.

UPDATE: Aug. 21, 2026

After a one-week hiccup, Novo Nordisk’s Wegovy pill regained its momentum last week with its largest prescription rate since it was launched in January. There were more than 176,000 prescriptions for the pill in the period, according to data gathered by IQVIA and cited in a note by Citi. 

The oral treatment now accounts for 35% of total Wegovy prescriptions, which is up from 33% the previous week, analysts from Citi said in their weekly update to investors.

Meanwhile, Eli Lilly’s oral GLP-1 Foundayo, which had been on a steady five-week climb, backtracked, with a drop-off from 38,928 prescriptions in the prior period to 36,620 in the latest week.

The movements for the two oral treatments contributed to overall market share adjustments for the companies' diabetes and obesity medicines. While Lilly made a 0.1% gain to 56.7%, Novo increased its market share by 0.3% to 37.1%.  

UPDATE: Aug. 14, 2026

Despite its leading position in the oral GLP-1 market, Novo Nordisk's Wegovy pill seems to be hitting a market share ceiling. For months now, shares of total prescriptions for Wegovy pill within the entire Wegovy franchise have struggled to break through the one-third mark.

While share of oral semaglutide within all Wegovy scripts hit 35% in our previous update, it fell back to 33% last week, as Wegovy pill scripts dropped to about 163K, down from a high of roughly 172K the week prior, according to IQVIA data cited by Citi. 

Total Wegovy scripts, including the original injectable, declined 1.1% sequentially to about 495.5K. As a result, Novo yielded about 0.7 percentage point in obesity market share to Eli Lilly's Zepbound last week based on the IQVIA data. The split stood at 39.9% and 60.1% between Novo and Lilly.

Meanwhile, Lilly's Foundayo continued its upward trajectory with 38,928 total scripts, representing another step up from its previous record of 34,219 set the week prior.

UPDATE: Aug. 7, 2026

Prescriptions for Eli Lilly's Foundayo continue to build, jumping 16% sequentially to 34,219 the previous week, according to IQVIA data cited by Citi. The oral GLP-1 med has been on a roll lately as it appears to celebrate four weeks of consecutive growth in total scripts. However, as Citi noted, there's still a potential gap in IQVIA's capture of telehealth data, and it's not clear how much of the scripts growth was from IQVIA getting better at including those data, or, if the actual growth was much faster in telehealth channels.

This week, Lilly's reported Foundayo sales for the second quarter—$98 million in total, including $67 million in the U.S.—disappointed many. As CEO David Ricks noted on an earnings call, Lilly began broad direct-to-consumer marketing to raise consumer awareness after securing commercial access across the three major pharmacy benefit managers in June. Besides, The Medicare GLP-1 Bridge program went live on July 1, offering coverage for certain weight-loss medications, including Foundayo, for a $50 copayment per month. Ilya Yuffa, president of Lilly USA and global customer capabilities, said the company is "starting to see an inflection point on Foundayo now."

As for Novo Nordisk's Wegovy pill, total scripts recorded by IQVIA have been largely flat with small upticks in the past two weeks, having reached roughly 172K in the previous week. The oral version of semaglutide now makes up 35% of total Wegovy scripts, which take up about 40.6% of the U.S. obesity market share, as Lilly's Zepbound remains the leader. 

UPDATE: July 31, 2026

The small inflection point we noticed two weeks ago regarding Eli Lilly's Foundayo does not appear to be a flash in the pan. Weekly total prescriptions for the small molecule reached 29,388, a new high for the oral GLP-1 receptor agonist after three weeks of consecutive growth, according to IQVIA data cited by Citi. 

As IQVIA may be missing some scripts from telehealth channels, we will get a clearer picture of Foundayo's launch progress when Lilly reports its second-quarter earnings on Wednesday, Aug. 5. Analysts at Jefferies have been modeling $71 million in U.S. sales for the quarter based on IQVIA data.

Meanwhile, Novo Nordisk's Wegovy pill remains far ahead in the oral GLP-1 race with total scripts also hitting a new record of about 171,700, according to Citi. The number represents 1.1% growth from its previous best recorded during the prior week.

Coincidentally, the entire GLP-1 class also saw its total scripts grow 1.1% sequentially across diabetes and obesity uses. Lilly's Zepbound regained some lost ground with total scripts up 1.9% week over week. That's compared to Wegovy, which now makes up 40.6% of the obesity market after a 0.2% sequential decline in total scripts. 

Novo reports earnings on the same day as Lilly, Aug. 5.

UPDATE: July 24, 2026

After a post-holiday lull, prescriptions for GLP-1s have more than bounced back. Weekly prescriptions for Novo Nordisk's Wegovy pill and Eli Lilly's Foundayo reached new highs during the previous week, collecting 169,800 and 26,760, respectively, according to IQVIA data cited by Citi. The two oral drugs' previous records were about 161.5K and 24.3K, respectively. 

Other GLP-1 drugs also enjoyed a boost, as total GLP-1 scripts across obesity and diabetes increased 6.6% sequentially, according to Citi.

From the obesity front, scripts for Lilly's Zepbound rose 7.7% sequentially to about 710K. The GLP-1/GIP dual agonist conceded 0.6 percentage points of market share to Novo but remains ahead of the game with a 58.9% share. That's compared to a 10.5% week-over-week scripts expansion for Novo's Wegovy, which mounted to about 495.5K. In that basket, about 34% belonged to Wegovy pill.

UPDATE: July 17, 2026

Following the Independence Day holiday, the overall GLP-1 market was down 5.1% week over week as measured by total prescriptions across obesity and diabetes uses, according to IQVIA data cited by Citi.

In the obesity field specifically, total scripts for Eli Lilly's Zepbound shrank by 3.1% sequentially to a little below 660K, while Novo Nordisk's Wegovy dipped 4.4% to about 448.5K.

Against this backdrop, Lilly's oral Foundayo seemed to enjoy a small inflection point, with a total 24,303 scripts notably breaking away from its roughly 20K level in the prior five weeks.  

Meanwhile, joining the bigger trend, Wegovy pill scripts dropped to 147.5K during the week, versus about 153K the prior week or 161.5K at its peak. But the contribution of the oral version to the overall Wegovy scripts remained stable at around a third, per Citi's note. 

UPDATE: July 10, 2026

The launch of Eli Lilly’s Foundayo remains “muted,” with weekly prescriptions flat over the last five weeks, analysts from Jefferies said in a July 10 note. The analysis is based on data collected by IQVIA.

In the 13th week of Foundayo’s launch, IQVIA reported 19,550 prescriptions, down for the third straight week after peaking at Week 10 with 21,648 prescriptions. The figure also comes in significantly shy of the Week 13 launch of Novo’s Wegovy pill (more than 105K scripts) and Lilly’s injected obesity treatment Zepbound (59K), but ahead of Novo’s injected Wegovy (13K).

Meanwhile, weekly scripts for Wegovy pill ticked slightly upward sequentially to about 153K, although they still lag behind the drug’s peak of more than 161K.

Jefferies points out that CVS was the last of the big three PBMs to provide coverage of Foundayo, starting on June 1. By contrast, Wegovy had full coverage at the first week of its launch.

While Jefferies’ $71 million quarterly sales projection for Foundayo sits significantly below Wall Street consensus of $130 million, the team still believes that the Lilly med can reach the consensus revenue estimate of $1.2 billion for 2026.

UPDATE: July 6, 2026

For a month now, weekly prescriptions for Eli Lilly's Foundayo have been hovering at around 20,000. In other words, three months into its market debut, the non-peptide GLP-1 receptor agonist was still at the same script level that Novo Nordisk's Wegovy pill had achieved in two to three weeks post-launch.

For the week ended on June 26, Foundayo's total scripts dipped about 4% sequentially to 19,830, according to IQVIA data cited by Jefferies. During the same period, scripts were also down about 2% for oral Wegovy, reaching about 149,000.

In a July 4 report, Jefferies analysts modeled about $71 million in U.S. sales during Foundayo's debut quarter from April to June, versus the team's previous estimate of $85 million in a June 26 report. Wall Street's consensus currently has the number at $130 million. To reach its estimate, Jefferies used an illustrative calculation based on the IQVIA data, with certain assumptions regarding pricing, dosing and stocking.

While Lilly still lags Novo on the oral GLP-1 battlefield, the Indianapolis pharma has maintained a majority 59.5% share of the overall obesity market, according to IQVIA's prescription data.  

As Novo's injectable Wegovy gained about 0.2% scripts (roughly 500) to reach 315,000 for the period, Lilly's Zepbound expanded by 1%, including 375,000 (+3,500) from Zepbound autoinjector and 289,000 (+2,000) from Zepbound DTC Vial+KwikPen.

UPDATE: June 29, 2026

Likely thanks to the Juneteenth federal holiday, prescriptions for both Novo Nordisk's Wegovy pill and Eli Lilly's Foundayo were lower compared with their highest. For the week ended on June 19, Foundayo logged 20,594 total scripts, down from 21,648 the prior week, according to IQVIA data cited by Jefferies. 

For oral Wegovy, the numbers were about 152,000 for the June 19 week, a roughly 9,500 (5.9%) decrease from the prior week. 

As Jefferies' analysts noted, most GLP-1 scripts were down or rather flat in their weekly comparisons. Injectable Wegovy added about 1,000 (0.3%) scripts, landing at 315,000. Mounjaro essentially saw no change, at 804,000.

Lilly has previously noted that it takes time to build awareness for Foundayo as a new brand, whereas Novo benefits from familiarity with the Wegovy moniker. 

Meanwhile, Sandoz just announced that the FDA has accepted its generic tirzepatide autoinjector applications, covering all indications of Lilly's Mounjaro and Zepbound. We'll see how the availability of a generic injectable version shakes up the oral market. 

UPDATE: June 18, 2026

Name recognition and "familiarity" with Novo Nordisk's oral Wegovy has contributed to its rapid uptake in its battle with Lilly's oral GLP-1 Foundayo, according to Spherix analyst Jim Hickey, who conducts monthly surveys with doctors who prescribe the treatments. See Fierce's story on Hickey's analysis here.

UPDATE: June 12, 2026

The share of Novo Nordisk's Wegovy pill among total Wegovy scripts appears to have reached a plateau, hovering around one-third over the past few weeks. The latest number for the week ended on June 5 was 33%, compared with 30%, 32% and 31% in the prior weeks, according to Citi. 

Meanwhile, the obesity market share split between Wegovy and Eli Lilly's Zepbound has been relatively stable at around 40% to 42%, as the Indianapolis pharma's oral Foundayo makes up only a small portion of the market even though its own scripts continue to build. 

Wegovy's total scripts were up 9.8% on a weekly basis, reaching nearly 484,500. Within this haul, Wegovy pill contributed roughly 159,000, the oral version's highest since its launch. The drug's previous highest was 146,000 before dipping to 134,000 in our last update.

Zepbound's scripts also grew week over week by 9.3%, nearing 667,400 for the week. During the same period, IQVIA tracked slightly shy of 20,000 scripts from Foundayo in its ninth week on the market, compared with nearly 17,000 the prior week. 

Thanks to the expansion of the oral version, Wegovy overall now commands 42.1% of the obesity market. Tracing backwards, its share has been climbing steadily, clocking in at 41.9%, 41.2%, 41.4%, 40.5%, 40.4%, 42.6% and 40.4% in the past few weeks.

UPDATE: June 8, 2026

It took just over five months for Novo Nordisk’s Wegovy pill to log 3 million total U.S. prescriptions, underscoring “one of the strongest US pharmaceutical launches by volume on record,” the company announced in a June 7 press release. Meanwhile, Eli Lilly’s rival Foundayo has still yet to achieve more than 17,000 prescriptions, according to a June 5 note from Citi analysts.  

Using data from IQVIA, the analysts tracked 16,982 Foundayo prescriptions as of the drug's eighth week on the market since its April launch. However, the Citi team emphasizes that “there may be a gap in telehealth capture,” as Lilly has previously confirmed to the analysts around 20,000 Foundayo scripts since its launch. Foundayo has been floating around this range for several weeks now since hitting 16,698 at week six, the data show.

Meanwhile, Novo’s Wegovy pill was at 73,544 prescriptions by the time it had hit the same eight-week marker in its own launch. The drug had picked up one million prescriptions 12 weeks after launching and nabbed an additional two million prescriptions in the following ten weeks, Novo said in its release. At its three million total, one prescription is filled roughly every five seconds, the company pointed out in its release. 

Either way, IQVIA’s data suggests a preference for oral formulations in the wider GLP-1 market, with oral Wegovy prescriptions now contributing 30% of total Wegovy scripts, according to the Citi analysts. The oral offering may be driving a wider market for the obesity treatments as well, with Novo explaining in its recent release that more than 80% of its new prescriptions for the Wegovy pill come from people new to GLP-1 therapy. 

June 2 findings from Spherix Global Insights second the notion that oral GLP-1 pills are expanding the overall treatment pool and drawing in a “massive wave of new patients,” the company said in an emailed release. In oral Wegovy’s first four weeks on the market earlier this year, 73% of surveyed primary care physician reported prescribing the med, with over 98% who haven’t yet prescribed it planning to within the next six months, Spherix found. 

“Novo Nordisk’s early performance has set an exceptionally high bar for the competition,” Spherix’s gastroenterology franchise head, Jim Hickey, commented.

On a weekly basis, however, total GLP-1 prescriptions were trending downward over the week of June 1, falling 5.7% week-over-week, Citi analysts noted. Other than the continued rollout of Lilly and Novo’s respective weight loss pills, the analysts cited the effect of the Trump administration’s “most favored nation” pricing policies as a key future event that they think could impact total prescriptions. 

UPDATE: June 1, 2026

In its seventh week on the market, which ended May 22, Eli Lilly’s obesity pill Foundayo continued to track below the pace of Novo Nordisk’s rival Wegovy pill at the same point in its launch.

At the same time, analysts at Jefferies and Citi again flagged caveats that could be skewing the numbers, with the Jefferies team espousing confidence that Lilly’s oral GLP-1 can still meet consensus sales projections for both the second quarter and 2026 as a whole. 

Breaking down the numbers, the Jefferies team put seventh-week total Foundayo prescriptions lower versus the previous week at roughly 11,700, with the clarification that the data’s source, IQVIA, had to use a “best-estimate” tally for the latest week’s prescription trends. 

That trend remains “numerically lower” than the course charted by Novo’s Wegovy pill, which racked up an impressive 67,000 prescriptions in its seventh week, although Foundayo’s performance still tracks ahead of Novo’s injectable Wegovy and Lilly’s first obesity incretin med Zepbound at the same point in their respective rollouts, the analyst team said. 

Lilly has suggested it expects the market for oral obesity meds to “develop over time” and has also cited the time needed to build new brand awareness for Foundayo, according to Jefferies, which added that the Lilly pill’s commercial reimbursement “appears to be ramping more slowly” compared to oral Wegovy. Lilly has confirmed that coverage of Foundayo through CVS Caremark, the United States’ biggest PBM, will begin this week. 

Despite those apparent growing pains, the analysts at Jefferies called Foundayo’s ability to meet consensus sales estimates in the near-term and for the full year as “doable.” The analysts currently predict that Lilly’s oral weight loss med will garner $145 million in the second quarter on the way to a $1.6 billion haul for the full year. 

Consensus estimates are tracking for Q2 and full-year Foundayo sales of $136 million and $1.2 billion, respectively, according to Jefferies. 

On that note, analysts at Citi, have repeatedly warned that IQVIA’s prescription data may be failing to account for telehealth referrals, citing comments from Lilly executives on the total patients they were tracking as of the company’s Q1 earnings call. For its part, Citi placed the total number of Foundayo scripts for the week ending May 22 at roughly 16,000, based on the IQVIA stats. 

By comparison, Novo’s Wegovy pill clocked some 146,000 total scripts over that same seven-day stretch, per Citi. Citi once more flagged that Novo’s Wegovy pill is making up a growing portion of overall semaglutide obesity prescriptions, which the team said points to “preferences for oral formulations.”

UPDATE: May 22, 2026

With both Novo Nordisk’s and Eli Lilly’s oral GLP-1s establishing their footing in the U.S. obesity market, the companies’ respective Wegovy pill and orforglipron tablet Foundayo are making their mark on prescription trends for a class previously confined primarily to injectables.

Looking at the past four weeks, total U.S. GLP-1 prescriptions were up 3.6%, compared to 1.8% at the same time last year, analysts at Citi wrote in a Friday note to clients, citing script tracking data from IQVIA. The Citi team attributed that momentum to the ability of Novo’s and Lilly’s new oral launches to “broaden and reshape the market” for obesity incretin drugs.

As of the week ended May 15, IQVIA logged nearly 17,000 prescriptions for Lilly’s Foundayo, which debuted on April 9. As in prior weeks, the Citi analysts caveated that IQVIA’s data may be missing key prescribing stats from telehealth channels, flagging Lilly executives’ comments during an earnings call at the end of last month that there were then roughly 20,000 patients on the new oral therapy.

Conversely, Novo’s Wegovy pill has recorded roughly 142,000 prescriptions as of last week, according to Citi’s note.

In an apparent sign of the new oral option's popularity, the analysts flagged that oral Wegovy now comprises 31% of total prescriptions for the brand, which is otherwise administered as an injection. The Citi team noted that this trend could signal “preferences for oral formulations.”

Meanwhile, scoping out the broader U.S. GLP-1 market over the past four weeks, Lilly’s tirzepatide brand—which includes both Zepbound for obesity and Mounjaro for Type 2 diabetes—now holds a 54.8% share compared to a 47% piece of the pie last year. Novo’s U.S. market share for semaglutide has remained “relatively flat” over that stretch and clocked in at 37.4%, per Citi.

Week over week, total GLP-1 prescriptions were down a little less than 1% in the U.S. Looking at obesity specifically, Citi’s analysts flagged a 2.1% tirzepatide prescription decline versus last week, while Novo’s Wegovy prescriptions tracked at a positive 1.8%.

Aside from both companies' oral GLP-1 launches continuing to add texture to the market, the analysts noted that the effect of the Trump administration’s “most favored nation” pricing policies on Novo’s and Lilly’s drugs could boost overall prescriptions for the class. 

UPDATE: May 15, 2026

Total prescriptions for Eli Lilly’s Foundayo reached 10,248 for the week that ended May 8, up from 7,335 the prior week, according to IQVIA data cited by Citi. While still on the rise, Foundayo’s growth pace continued to lag behind that of Novo Nordisk’s Wegovy pill during the same stage of their launch. 

Wegovy’s total scripts rose by 1.3% week over week to nearly 446,000, as its share in the obesity GLP-1 market climbed 0.1 percentage point to 40.5%, according to Citi.

However, Wegovy’s growth apparently didn’t come from its oral formulation. Wegovy pill scripts landed at about 137,000 for the week, down from roughly 143,000 the prior week, marking the first time that the pill's scripts have fallen since the oral launch in early January.

Scripts from the Wegovy pill made up 31% of total Wegovy scripts for the period, down 2 percentage points from the previous week. Still, Citi analysts argued that this roughly one-third of share “suggests preferences for oral formulations.”

Even as Wegovy gained ground, Lilly’s Zepbound remained the obesity market leader, with 59.5% share, as its nearly 656,000 scripts marked 0.8% growth week over week. 

UPDATE: May 8, 2026

As Eli Lilly’s Foundayo finds its footing on the market, Novo Nordisk’s own Wegovy pill—which got a three-month head start to launch over its rival this year—is starting to illuminate just how significant an oral GLP-1 may be to the lucrative obesity drug landscape. 

In the fourth week since its April 9 debut in the U.S., Lilly’s Foundayo has generated 7,335 total prescriptions, analysts at Citi wrote in a note to clients Friday, citing prescribing stats from IQVIA. 

That ramp-up looks slower on paper than that enjoyed by the Wegovy pill during its initial rollout, but the Citi team cautioned that there may be a gap in IQVIA data linked to telehealth prescriptions for Lilly’s tablet. They pointed to comments from Lilly executives late last week indicating that there were now some 20,000 patients on Foundayo, with the company noting that telehealth platforms were generating some 35% of the oral GLP-1 medicine’s current launch volume. 

The analysts acknowledged that Lilly’s early Foundayo prescription trends “continue to build,” while adding that they “look for further growth to develop the oral competitive market.” 

During its earnings call last week, Lilly added that upcoming coverage secured at major pharmacy benefit managers should come online by the middle of May, providing a likely sizeable tailwind to Foundayo’s trajectory. 

As for Novo, the company logged some 440,410 Wegovy prescriptions on the week that ended May 1, with oral Wegovy now making up 33% of those total obesity referrals, per the Citi analysts, who said that trend could reflect “preferences for oral formulations.”

The update on the oral obesity numbers comes after Novo earlier this week reported that the Wegovy pill generated 2.26 billion Danish kroner (around $355 million) in its first quarter on the U.S. market. 

For its part, Foundayo will likely need to start generating around 22,000 prescriptions a week in order to hit current consensus forecasts of $160 million in second-quarter sales, RBC Capital Markets’ Trung ​Huynh said this week, as cited by Reuters. 

UPDATE: May 4, 2026

With three weeks of data on Lilly’s oral GLP-1 launch in obesity now on the books, the dimensions of Foundayo’s rollout—and its critical comparison to that of Novo Nordisk’s Wegovy pill—are coming into focus. 

In its third week on the U.S. market, which ended April 24, Foundayo generated some 5,600 prescriptions, analysts at Jefferies wrote in a May 1 note to clients. That level of adoption is numerically lower than the stats recorded by the Wegovy pill in its third week, when prescriptions for the oral obesity med came in at around 26,100, per the note. 

Nevertheless, almost all of Foundayo’s recorded performance stems from cash pay channels, according to the Jefferies team, with commercial access via insurance set to come online by the middle of this month, which will likely give Foundayo a substantial boost in uptake. 

The team acknowledged that Foundayo’s reimbursement “appears to be ramping more slowly vs oral Wegovy’s.” 

Overall, the analysts described Foundayo as “off to a solid start,” and estimate the drug will generate $146 million in the second quarter and $1.6 billion for all of 2026. That compares to consensus forecasts of $134 million and $1.2 billion, respectively. 

Lilly told the Jefferies team that, as of week three of its launch, some 45% of Foundayo prescriptions were coming through its direct-to-patient channel LillyDirect, alongside 35% of referrals from telehealth providers and the remaining 20% coming from traditional retail venues. 

During an earnings call with analysts last week, Lilly executives noted that there were around 20,000 patients on Foundayo in the U.S. The drug was approved April 1. 

As for Novo’s pill, oral Wegovy lassoed around 135,000 total prescriptions during the week that ended April 24, according to the Jefferies notes. 

UPDATE: April 24, 2026

Eli Lilly’s oral GLP-1 obesity treatment Foundayo has attracted 3,707 prescriptions though its second week on the market, lagging far behind the pace of Novo Nordisk’s GLP-1 pill Wegovy, which drew 18,410 prescriptions though its second week on the market in January. 

The results were made available by Jefferies from healthcare analytics firm IQVIA and are good through the week ending on April 17.

With the result, Lilly’s shares dipped by 4% on Friday, compared to a 7% gain for Novo.

Foundayo’s launch so far does compare favorably to that of Novo’s injected Wegovy, which numbered 1,578 prescriptions through two weeks when it reached the market in the U.S. but falls short of Lilly’s Zepbound pen, which counted 7,292 prescriptions through its second week.

In its note to investors, analysts from Jefferies called the result “disappointing vs. expectations."

Brand recognition has played a role, according to Bernstein analyst Courtney Breen, who said that online searches for GLP-1 drugs peaked during Wegovy’s launch, potentially boosting demand.

UPDATE: April 21, 2026

Eli Lilly’s oral GLP-1 Foundayo is off to a solid launch, drawing 1,390 prescriptions in its first week on the market, according to tracking figures from IQVIA and presented by Jefferies. The tabulation is from the week starting April 6. This compares to the 3,071 prescriptions Novo Nordisk garnered during its Wegovy pill launch week in January.

While Foundayo came up short in this oral GLP-1 launch week comparison, it did exceed the number of prescriptions recorded in the first week of the launch of both Lilly’s injected Zepbound (1,100) and Novo’s injected version of Wegovy (768).

In a note to clients, analysts with Jefferies cautioned that comparisons can be “tricky” given that oral Wegovy was launched at the start of the year and that initial capture rates from IQVIA are “volatile” and may not include product sampling. 

“Overall, we think Foundayo’s initial scripts look excellent,” the Jefferies team wrote, adding that it is modeling Foundayo’s sales to reach $1.6 billion this year, compared to a consensus of $1.5 billion, with its peak annual sales topping out at $30 billion versus the consensus of $26 billion. 

“We think the real opportunity for Foundayo is ex-U.S., given its clear advantages on scale, distribution and [cost of goods sold],” Jefferies wrote.

data.title: Genentech amplifies breast cancer conversations in new campaign
data.description:
Genentech is turning up the volume on breast cancer conversations in its “About Damn Time” campaign with Breastcancer.org and other advocacy partners. 

“About Damn Time” focuses on the often-overlooked years after initial intensive treatment of women with (HR)-positive, human epidermal growth factor receptor 2 (HER2)-negative early breast cancer. That experience can be defined by follow-up hormone therapy or long term treatment and a new world of uncertainty as patients navigate a pressing fear of disease recurrence.

“Progress in breast cancer care cannot only be measured by how long people live, but by how well they live," said Charlotte Owens, M.D., SVP and head of U.S. medical at Genentech, in an Oct. 1 release. "As a physician and caregiver, I say it’s About Damn Time we focus on caring for the whole patient, not just treating the disease."

Through the campaign, Genentech looks to “empower women with breast cancer to speak with their care teams about the realities of long-term treatment so they can get the support they need to thrive in the years that follow,” Owens added. 

The company and patient-focused nonprofit Breastcancer.org worked with Young Survival Coalition, Latinas Contra Cancer and TOUCH, The Black Breast Cancer Alliance to create a dedicated webpage filled with resources and tools to prepare for long-term care, as well as stories from other survivors. 

Related

Novartis survey shines a light on hidden realities of women's conversations about breast health

In a two-minute campaign video associated with the project, breast cancer survivors Brooklyn, Alice, Megan-Claire, Alicia and Dani come together to discuss the things “no one prepares you for.” All five women are real breast cancer survivors who have been compensated for their time, with the video also linking each woman’s social media handle. 

“It’s About Damn Time we get louder about the quiet parts of breast cancer—with honest stories, practical tools, and support from women who’ve been there. Because every woman’s experience is different,” Alice says in the video. 

“But no woman should have to figure it out alone,” Brooklyn adds. 

More than 225,000 women in the U.S are expected to be diagnosed with HR-positive/ HER2-negative breast cancer this year, according to Genentech. The breast cancer subtype is the most common form of the disease and makes up some 70% of all cases. After initial treatment with surgery, chemotherapy or radiation, hormone therapy is typically recommended for at least five years to prevent recurrence. 

“Breast cancer care doesn’t end when initial treatment stops. For many, it’s just entering its longest phase,” Breastcancer.org founder and chief medical officer Marisa C. Weiss, M.D., added in the release. “We have to acknowledge it, study it and offer people solutions to live the lives they deserve.” 

Genentech markets a plethora of breast cancer treatments, including Itovebi for HR positive, HER2 negative PIK3CA-mutated breast cancer. This year, Genentech’s parent company Roche made first place on PatientView’s oncology corporate reputation ranking, reflecting high marks from 505 cancer patient groups surveyed.

data.title: J&J finds women not connecting menopause to eye health changes
data.description:
Hot flashes, mood and sleep disturbances are common themes for menopause: But vision changes are not as well recognized on the list of common symptoms. Now, J&J is looking to highlight this often-overlooked issue. 

Published as part of Menopause Awareness Month in October, the new survey from Ipsos for J&J polled 6,000 women across multiple countries and found that 40% of them did not connect eye changes with the menopause transition.

This comes even though 66% of those surveyed said they have experienced dry, gritty or irritated eyes, while 60% have experienced blurred vision.

J&J also found that just 18% of respondents have talked about these changes with an eye care professional.

As part of the new survey, J&J is also continuing to tap Naomi Watts, actress and founder of Stripes Beauty, who is sharing her eye health journey whilst also “encouraging women to include vision in their midlife wellness routine,” according to a statement.

“We’re talking more openly about menopause, but eye health is still too often left out,” said Watts in a release. 

“I want women to know they don’t have to quietly work around changes like dry eyes or blurry vision. An eye exam is a simple step that can help them understand their eye health options and feel more in control.”

Related

Johnson & Johnson directs a new campaign for aging eyes with Naomi Watts in the spotlight

J&J’s Vision unit currently markets a host of eye health products, including a whole range of contact lenses as well as surgical products.  

Eye symptoms associated with menopause can include dry or irritated eyes, blurry near vision, headaches, or needing to hold reading material farther away, J&J said. 

The company is asking women to note any of those changes and report them to their doctor. There is also a new accompanying  website and quiz from J&J Vision to help women understand whether they may be seeing eye changes through menopause.

data.title: Real Chemistry adds MaestroHCP to conduct omnichannel campaigns
data.description:
Real Chemistry has created an artificial intelligence-enabled platform to improve a manual, fragmented stage of the omnichannel marketing process. 

The product, MaestroHCP, grew out of recognition of a limitation of next best action decision engines, Elizabeth Beringer, president of Real Chemistry Media, told Fierce. Drugmakers have developed the tools to inform where sales reps focus their time. However, Beringer said the engines miss the nuance of non-personal promotion.

“We had a client where the next best action engine said, ‘hey, this doctor should go to the website and read about efficacy.’ However, we can't say, ‘hey, doctor, go to the website,’” Beringer said. “We need to fill in all of the gaps of which channel is going to be most likely to get the physician to come to the page.”

Real Chemistry designed MaestroHCP to help fill in those gaps. MaestroHCP handles “the last mile between a next best action decision engine and all of the media investment, CRM—the other channels that can be orchestrated through partners, like the publishers that we're working with,” Beringer said. 

The product has optional AI capabilities. The AI-powered engine “makes real-time decisions about which channels, which tactics, which creative combinations are going to move the needle,” Beringer said. While Beringer has “great confidence that [the AI engine] will outperform traditional one-to-many sequence setup,” MaestroHCP supports marketers who have reservations about trusting the technology. 

“One of the biggest criticisms I always hear is, ‘I don't know what's in the black box. I don't know what the inputs are. I don't know how to fine-tune it,’” Beringer said. By supporting traditional sequence setup and allowing users to apply AI to individual steps in the journey, Beringer believes MaestroHCP can help build trust in the technology and drive increased use of the AI-powered decision engine.

Real Chemistry has developed the product with Amazon Web Services, creating two models that clients can use with MaestroHCP. Clients have the option to use their own AI models in MaestroHCP. Real Chemistry’s models are “truly custom,” Beringer said, not just relabeled versions of a tool such as Claude, and the team continues to improve orchestration. 

“We’re really fine-tuning the investment decisioning and making sure that we have the ability to do more with less,” Beringer said. “More and more pharma marketers are coming to us and saying, ‘hey, we're being asked to keep our budget flat but produce more revenue. How can you help us do this?’ And Maestro is definitely one of our biggest answers right now.”

data.title: For Rare Disease Marketing, Precision Starts with the Care Pathway
data.description:
Written by Joe Post, Client Lead

For rare disease brands, traditional media planning can fall short when it relies on broad audience segments, conventional HCP lists, or channel-by-channel activation. The relevant patient population may be small and dispersed, while the route to diagnosis can span multiple specialties, referrals, tests, payers, caregivers, and advocacy communities.

For marketers, that complexity creates a familiar challenge: knowing the right audience is out there, but not always knowing where they are in the journey, who is influencing their next step, or which intervention can make a meaningful difference.

As nearly one in two new pharmaceutical approvals is now tied to an orphan or rare disease condition, the need for a more specialized model is increasing. CMI Media Group has formally launched its Rare Disease Center of Excellence (COE) to address that gap—helping marketers move from planning for scale to planning for precision.

Finding the “needle in a haystack”

Rare disease marketing is often described as finding a needle in a haystack. But the task is not simply locating a patient or prescriber; it is understanding the signals and relationships that can lead to diagnosis and appropriate treatment.

The COE starts by mapping the care pathway and the signals within it. Claims data, procedure codes, diagnostic test data, and custom research from CMI's Audience Intelligence team can help reveal referral patterns, diagnostic events, and other meaningful moments along the journey. 

Advanced HCP reclassification helps distinguish physicians who may identify or refer a patient from those who prescribe, allowing media strategies to reflect each clinician's role.

The approach is complemented by engagement with key opinion leaders, medical societies, advocacy groups, and other partners across the rare disease ecosystem. Together, these capabilities can help address symptom under-recognition, fragmented care, and payer hurdles that may delay diagnosis.

Connecting a journey that rarely happens in a straight line

Rare disease marketers are often tasked with solving multiple challenges at once: helping HCPs recognize an unfamiliar condition, supporting appropriate referral and testing, educating patients and caregivers who may have spent years searching for answers, and ultimately connecting those efforts around the same journey.

The COE is designed to bring those perspectives together. Rather than treating HCP, patient, and caregiver strategies as separate worksteams, teams can plan around the moments where their needs and behaviors intersect – creating a more connected experience across the path to diagnosis and treatment.

Bridging boutique expertise and agency scale

The purpose of the COE is to eliminate a choice that rare disease clients have historically faced: working with a specialized boutique that offers high-touch therapeutic expertise or a scaled agency with sophisticated data infrastructure, technology, and buying power.

Rare disease brands should not have to choose between specialized attention and scaled capability. CMI’s framework brings those capabilities together through dedicated talent, AI-enabled tools, tailored data integration, and curated media ecosystems. That combination enables teams to build highly specific strategies while maintaining the operational scale, activation capabilities, and efficiencies required to support a brand over time.

The COE builds on the agency’s experience launching more than 67 rare disease brands across nephrology, oncology, ophthalmology, cardiology, hematology, immunology, pulmonology, and rheumatology.

"Rare disease challenges some of the assumptions we've been taught to make as marketers. The most efficient tactic on paper isn't always the one that will find the patient who needs you. Sometimes precision means going deeper and doubling down in places where the numbers alone might tell you to pull back. That requires data, but it also requires experience and judgment – and an understanding of what's at stake for the patient behind every signal," says Joe Post, Client Lead, Engagement Strategy at CMI Media Group.

As AI accelerates, the human perspective matters more

AI enabled tools can help teams identify patterns across complex data, surface potential connections, and accelerate planning and optimization. But as technology becomes more powerful, human judgment becomes more – not less – important.

This is particularly true in rare disease. Behind every data point may be a patient or caregiver managing uncertainty, misdiagnosis, years of searching for answers, or an unfamiliar treatment decision. Understanding that experience requires more than an algorithm. It requires therapeutic expertise, content, and empathy.

Any use of AI in this space should be grounded in privacy-preserving practices, appropriate data governance, de-identification, applicable consent requirements, and human oversight. Technology should help teams understand systems and pathways—not attempt to expose individual patients. CMI’s use of AI-enabled tools sits alongside the expertise needed to interpret signals responsibly.

Measuring progress beyond reach

For rare disease brands, success cannot be defined by impressions or efficiency alone.

Measurement should reflect the problem the brand is actually trying to solve. Depending on the brand's objectives and available data, that may mean understanding whether the right HCPs are engaging, whether referral or testing behaviors are changing, whether patients and caregivers are finding meaningful support, or whether measurable friction along the journey is being reduced.

The Rare Disease COE is currently active across CMI Media Group’s internal planning teams and new business initiatives. It brings specialized expertise so brands can spend less time navigating complexity – and more time focused on the decisions that can make a difference for the rare disease communities that they serve.

To learn more, visit cmimediagroup.com/services or contact [email protected].

data.title: Asahi Kasei wraps years of global dealmaking into a single brand
data.description:
After years of deal-driven global expansion, Asahi Kasei is rolling its pharma units up under a single brand and forging ahead with efforts to drive sales toward $2 billion by the end of the decade.

Tokyo-based Asahi has expanded globally through deals since 2020, when it put down roots in the U.S. by acquiring Veloxis Pharmaceuticals. In 2024, Asahi added Sweden’s Calliditas to its roster in a $1 billion deal. The conglomerate returned to the deal table in February, when it agreed to buy Germany’s Aicuris for about $920 million. 

The acquired biotechs retained their own branding—until now. Going forward, the units will all operate as Asahi Kasei Therapeutics, the name of the company’s existing Japanese pharma business. Integration establishes a unified global management structure for the pharmaceutical business, Asahi said. 

Bringing the units under a single global management structure “will allow us to make resource allocation decisions across the business rather than by company or geography,” Yoshikazu Aoki, global president of Asahi Kasei Therapeutics, said in a statement. Aoki added that the new structure provides “a stronger platform to pursue in-licensing opportunities.” 

Asahi is seeking deals to expand its pipeline and support continued growth. The company plans to invest about 40 billion Japanese yen ($250 million) in in-licensing over the next three years. In-licensing and additional M&A form part of Asahi’s strategy for growing revenues to 300 billion Japanese yen ($1.9 billion) by its 2030 financial year. 

The company focuses on specialty therapeutic areas, including immunology, nephrology, transplantation and infectious diseases. Asahi acquired the kidney transplant drug Envarsus XR in the Veloxis takeover. The company entered another kidney indication by acquiring Calliditas, which sells the immunoglobulin A nephropathy drug Tarpeyo. 

Buying Aicuris moved Asahi into infectious disease drug development. Aicuris receives royalties on sales of Prevymis, a cytomegalovirus drug licensed by Merck & Co., and has a pipeline of programs targeting infectious diseases, including herpes simplex virus.

data.title: Organon phones home with sci-fi themed Vtama campaign
data.description:
Organon is putting on its tinfoil hat to promote steroid-free atopic dermatitis and plaque psoriasis cream Vtama in a science fiction-themed education campaign aimed at healthcare practitioners. 

With the tagline “it’s not science fiction, its Skin Science,” Organon leans on the drug’s first-in-class clinical profile to make a memorable impression on HCPs and stand out in the dense medical dermatology market. 

“Marketing for products that treat chronic skin conditions so often focuses on freedom from those conditions, so we wanted to break that mold with bold, unexpected creative that would capture attention while reinforcing Vtama’s distinct clinical profile,” Organon’s head of U.S. dermatology marketing Ryan Billings explained to Fierce over email. 

To go with the tagline and the science fiction theme seen splayed across Organon’s Vtama webpage for HCPs, the company ran three video spots that feature a crew of aliens desperate to get their three-fingered hands on some Vtama.  

In “Beam Me Up,” patrons of a Nebraskan late-night diner are shaken up by the arrival of a UFO, which declares it has “detected an anomaly here on earth,” suggesting a “substance of great interest to us.” 

“We arrive in search of this innovative science,” the UFO announces, making it clear the object of its desire is one diner patron’s Vtama. Two aliens sitting inside the UFO hold out a two-finger peace sign, doubling as a ‘V’ sign as they chant “V-TAAA-MA!” in high-pitched alien voices. 
Vtama skin science campaign

The aliens and the UFO leave in peace after collecting the man’s Vtama, leaving him confused and Vtama-less. A voiceover listing the drug’s labeling details comes out slightly grainy, as if playing through a plane (or UFO) loudspeaker. Meanwhile, the UFO is orbiting outer space as the aircraft’s display screen analyzes a tube of Vtama. 

Similar science fiction tropes play out in the other two spots. In “Late Night Visitor,” a doctor working late at the dark office hears a noise, prompting her and a janitor to seek out the source of the shuffle with flashlights. They discover a chirping alien rifling through cabinets in search of Vtama, which the doctor hands over, agreeing that “the science, it’s fascinating."

After showing the satisfied alien checking over the Vtama in his UFO, the ad ends with a humorous shot of the janitor sighing as he picks up the mess the curious creature left behind.  

Related

FDA blesses atopic dermatitis label expansions for Organon's Vtama, Galderma's Nemluvio

In “Arrivals,” a police officer pulls up to a crowded scene, dotted with news vans and fascinated onlookers. No one can decipher the alien’s communication, until a woman in a lab coat pushes to the front. 

“Is this what you came for?” she shouts at the sky, holding out a tube of Vtama. An alien emerges from the UFO, confirming that yes, this is what it came for. 

Like the rest of the spots, “Arrivals” ends with the familiar swell of a science fiction-esque soundtrack and a bright Vtama logo drawn across the scene in a cinematic fashion. 

In creating the alien itself, Organon wanted to make the extraterrestrial appear “curious, a little innocent and completely fascinated by Vtama,” Billings said. The final result is a tiny, greenish creature with huge, sparkling eyes and a smiling appearance. If it’s sounding a bit like director Steven Spielberg, that’s by design—the team was looking to evoke the “tactile, slightly imperfect feeling of nostalgic sci-fi movies,” Billings noted. 

The campaign first launched at the American Academy of Dermatology Annual Meeting, debuting with an “immersive booth presence” and a “first-in-industry, distinctive crop circle visuals” Billings said. Organon is going with a multi-channel paid media approach including social-first video, interactive experiences and in-office education as well as through digital channels such as email, print, social media and other advertising avenues.  

“We know from market insights that healthcare professionals are actively seeking more engaging and culturally relevant content,” Billings said. “By leveraging science forward storytelling, this campaign is designed to break through the noise of a crowded environment to make complex science more memorable.” 

The company met with ten advisory boards with over 120 dermatologists and allergists to gauge those insights, revealing a “strong appetite for differentiated, science-led education,” he added. 

Related

Organon-commissioned survey finds 1 in 3 UK women feel their migraine pain not taken seriously

“Ultimately, this approach is about bridging the education gap,” Billings explained. “We want to capture attention, spark curiosity, and help clinicians see where Vtama could fit into their treatment decisions.”

Organon, a Merck spin-out that primarily focuses on women’s health and was bought out by Indian generics giant Sun Pharma earlier this year, took on Vtama in 2024 through its $1.2 billion Dermavant acquisition. The topical aryl hydrocarbon receptor (AhR) agonist first hit the market in 2022 for plaque psoriasis, adding on an atopic dermatitis indication in late 2024.

Last year, the medicine picked up $128 million in total sales. The drug has so far fallen short of its initial blockbuster ambitions and didn’t reach its $150 million sales target last year, but has a significant eligible patient population to crack in the U.S. with its latest atopic dermatitis nod including adults and children two years of age and older.

data.title: Tagrisso rival loses EU approval after AZ legal challenge
data.description:
The European Commission has revoked the EU marketing authorization for Hansoh Pharma’s lung cancer drug Aumseqa (aumolertinib) following a legal challenge from rival AstraZeneca.

The EC made the decision after the European Medicines Agency concluded that Hansoh partner SFL Pharma’s application from 2022 violated data protection rules by referencing AstraZeneca’s clinical data for Tagrisso, according to a Sept. 25 letter signed by the EC’s director-general for health and food safety, Sandra Gallina.

The EMA recommended approval for Aumseqa in November 2025 before the EGFR inhibitor was officially approved in February for the first-line treatment of EGFR-mutated non-small cell lung cancer, posing a direct threat to AZ’s blockbuster Tagrisso.

In a Sept. 27 announcement (PDF), Hansoh described the setback as “a procedural issue” that’s “not related to the quality, safety, efficacy or clinical value” of Aumseqa. According to Hansoh, the EC made the move after AZ sued the agency before the General Court of the EU. 

The Chinese company said it intends to resubmit the market application to the EMA using the original data package as soon as possible, and that it reserves all rights to challenge the revocation. 

“The Board is cautiously optimistic that a new marketing authorization can be obtained within a reasonably short timeframe,” Hansoh said, adding that “the EMA has indicated its willingness to shorten the standard assessment timeline.”

Despite its February approval in EU, Aumseqa has not generated any sales outside of China, where the drug received its first go-ahead in March 2020 under the brand name Ameile. The drug’s road to the EU market was long and winding, as reflected in the gap between its 2022 filing and 2026 approval.

Hansoh initially partnered with EQRx, whose dream of using China data to introduce cheaper cancer drugs to Western markets collapsed in 2023 after the FDA nixed that pathway. Hansoh, which did not have a presence in Europe, utilized SFL as the local face that inherited Aumseqa’s application. 

Related

Hansoh heralds China’s move from ‘follower’ to ‘frontrunner’ in biopharma race

Following its filing in 2022, Hansoh, at the request of European regulators, performed a European bridging study to complement its China data, which used first-generation EGFR inhibitor Iressa (gefitinib) as the comparator. 

To establish Aumseqa’s profile, Hansoh relied on clinical data from Tagrisso’s Flaura trial, which were at the time still under EU data protection, according to the EC’s determination letter.

Citing past communication between SFL and the EMA, the EC said, “without the reliance on the FLAURA clinical study data, the application dossier did not provide an adequate and sufficient basis for extrapolating the safety and efficacy of Aumseqa from an Asian to a European patient population.”

As the EC explains, drugs approved in EU enjoy an eight-year data protection period from the time of market authorization, where other applicants cannot refer to the preclinical or clinical results for another application. 

The protection around Tagrisso took effect on Feb. 4, 2016, and therefore was still in effect when Hansoh submitted its application. The protection expired in 2024, opening the door to a resubmission. 

The kerfuffle in the EU comes as AZ faces pressure from Aumseqa and other domestic EGFR inhibitors in China.

With nearly $3.8 billion sales in the first half of 2026, Tagrisso remains the world’s best-selling EGFR inhibitor. But as AZ’s CEO Pascal Soriot noted on the company’s second-quarter earnings call in July, the EGFR king is under two major competitive threats.

“One in China, which is the multiplicity of EGFR [inhibitors] in the market and very competitive market,” Soriot said.

Meanwhile, Johnson & Johnson’s combination of Rybrevant and Lazcluze is also coming after Tagrisso’s first-line share following a head-to-head phase 3 win.

data.title: Alnylam drafts football veteran for heart disease education push
data.description:
Alnylam Pharmaceuticals has teamed up with Pete Shaw, making the retired professional football player the star of its “Play by Play” educational heart disease initiative.

Shaw has transthyretin amyloid cardiomyopathy (ATTR-CM), a progressive heart disease treated by products including Alnylam’s Amvuttra. “Play by Play” tells Shaw’s story. In a six-minute video on the campaign website, Shaw, his wife Kari and his cardiologist Rajeev Mohan, M.D., discuss the symptoms leading up to the ATTR-CM diagnosis, his experience on Amvuttra and the implications for others.

“I want people to be aware of this disease,” Shaw says in the video. “About 4% of Black Americans carry the V122I gene. It is hereditary, so it could be in my family. I could pass it on to my children. My son had the hereditary gene variant. He didn't know and I didn't know.”

Starting with the “Play by Play” name, Alnylam’s campaign materials are dotted with parallels between sports and ATTR-CM. Just as “the power of football is built play by play,” the strength of Amvuttra is built on “making precise interventions where they matter,” Tolga Tanguler, chief commercialization officer at Alnylam, said in a statement.

The stage is set for more sporting analogies. While Shaw is kicking off the campaign, Alnylam called “Play by Play” a U.S. educational initiative featuring former professional athletes living with ATTR-CM. Across the campaign, the biotech will share personal stories to help people recognize ATTR-CM symptoms and to encourage informed conversations with healthcare professionals.

Alnylam is rolling out the campaign in the aftermath of a July sales guidance cut that raised questions about the prospects and positioning of Amvuttra in a market served by BridgeBio and Pfizer. While the rivals provide competition for Amvuttra, John Kennedy, Alnylam's TTR franchise global commercialization lead, made the case this month that there are benefits to having more companies raising awareness. 

“As there are more voices in the market, there’s better awareness, better understanding of the disease, we expect that diagnosis will happen more consistently and earlier, and that’s a good thing,” Kennedy said at a Wells Fargo event. “In fact, we intend to continue to facilitate that.”

data.title: Big Pharma's Big Brand: Regeneron
data.description:
Ronald Reagan was in the White House, Michael Jackson’s “Thriller” was pumping through Walkmans everywhere, and biotech was about to have a moment. It was the 1980s, and Genentech had just gone public.

Widely regarded as the first modern biotech company, Genentech’s debut set the wheels in motion for Leonard Schleifer, M.D., Ph.D., then an assistant professor of neurology at Cornell University.

“What about starting a company to take on neurologic diseases?” Schleifer had asked his mentor, he recalled in a 2019 interview with the Cornell Chronicle.

“That’s a stupid idea. Get back in the lab and do something good,” was his mentor’s response, the now-CEO said.

Last year, New York-based Regeneron pulled in $14.3 billion in annual revenue, reflecting blockbuster collaborations with Sanofi and Bayer and a diverse portfolio of innovative medicines across oncology, rare disease and more. In 2021, Schleifer’s “stupid idea” made him the top-paid CEO in biopharma and healthcare. Today, Schleifer still helms the company as CEO, while his co-founder George Yancopoulos, M.D., Ph.D., remains chief scientific officer.

A founder-led, multibillion-dollar pharma is a rarity in an industry dominated by centuries-old global companies. For Regeneron, its physician-scientist-led roots bleed into every part of its ongoing affairs.

In a new series, Fierce Pharma Marketing will interview Big Pharma marketing and communications leaders about how their companies are evolving their marketing cultures, defining what they stand for in 2026 and rethinking the industry’s reputation, public understanding and corporate role.

In our latest interview in the series, we talk with Christina Chan, senior vice president of corporate affairs at Regeneron.

‘Science-driven’ decisions 

“We’re still unique in the industry room,” Chan told Fierce Pharma Marketing. “There are not many like us.”

As Chan sees it, her team’s role at the company is to help the public understand the “science, innovation and people” behind the work that Regeneron’s scientists do every day. This involves making topics that are “very complex scientifically” more accessible. Despite the complexity of Regeneron’s work, Chan maintains that the public and Regeneron’s audiences “don’t need less science.”
Regeneron Christina Chan

“It’s more about different entry points,” she explained. 

One audio-focused entry point Regeneron has been exploring recently is its latest podcast series, “Science Illuminated.” The project transforms scientific imagery taken in Regeneron’s labs into a video-and-audio podcast format through a meditative series narrated by the company’s own staff engineer Michelle Mazzeo.

The concept allows Regeneron to distill its complex scientific topics into an immersive, calming experience and lets it “enter the conversation a little bit differently,” Chan said.

“We’ve always been science driven,” she explained. “It very much influences the way we make decisions.”

That carries through to the communications department as Chan and her team pair scientific insights with “new digital avenues” and media such as podcasting, resulting in something “deeply creative but also scientifically rigorous, and meets people where they’re consuming content.”

That, Chan said, is the “sweet spot” for Regeneron’s scientific storytelling.

Related

Regeneron podcast turns science learnings into immersive experience

Aside from “Science Illuminated,” Regeneron runs a host of unique online science messaging platforms, such as “Tech Trailblazers,” an educational series that features Regeneron scientists explaining their work alongside a young child who acts as a “scientific simplifier,” repeating the information in more casual, relatable language. The children featured in the videos are those of other Regeneron colleagues, bringing an all-in-the-family atmosphere to the labs.

The idea behind “Tech Trailblazers” stems from a common mantra of Yancopoulos, who often says “if you can’t describe it to a fifth grade, then you don’t really know it well enough,” according to Chan. “We took that to heart,” she said.

The series “humanizes” the science and comes from a social-forward, digitally conscious perspective. “Science Illuminated” takes a similar approach, meeting people in “different places of the storytelling.”

This, she said, is “where trust is built,” allowing people to understand the science as opposed to being put off by its complexity.

“That’s a big piece of our corporate responsibility,” she said. “How we approach the work, not just the work itself.”

Building trust through science

In 2026’s evolving digital landscape, marred by a pessimistic younger generation and politicized pharmaceutical topics, biopharma companies are making some inroads in rebuilding trust with a public that has long held a general distaste for the industry. Regeneron’s approach is to lean on science and make complex concepts easier for people to understand as a way to build that trust.

Within scientific discovery, “people can only understand the impact of that if they really understand what's underlying it,” Chan said. “That’s what we're always trying to translate, even from the Regeneron corporate brand perspective, to make that connection, to create that understanding.”

However, when it comes to establishing and maintaining trust, “it’s not just about what you say,” Chan said. “It’s what you do.”

One example of a Regeneron action that speaks volumes is its rare decision to offer its groundbreaking genetic hearing loss gene therapy Otarmeni at no cost in the U.S.

Approved in April under the FDA Commissioner’s National Priority Voucher program, Otarmeni made history as the first gene therapy for hearing loss related to variants in the OTOF gene.

The scientific achievement also marked a milestone for Regeneron and its emerging genetic medicines business as the company’s first approved gene therapy. What was once known as an "antibody company or biologics company" has been "building out our expertise across genetic medicine modalities" for the last eight years, Jonathon Whitton, Ph.D., of Regeneron’s genetic medicines program, told Fierce Biotech ahead of Otarmeni’s approval.

Gene therapies represent a major breakthrough in innovative science, but with the exorbitant cost of developing personalized treatments, they typically hit the market with a multimillion-dollar price tag. Along with Regeneron's Most Favored Nation drug pricing agreement, under which it pledged to lower the cost of its drugs on Medicaid and align the costs of its future therapies with prices "set in that defined group of other countries," the company opted to provide Otarmeni at no cost to clinically eligible individuals in the U.S.

“Otarmeni is a huge scientific leap and is representative of Regeneron’s approaches to continually push the boundaries of science to benefit humanity,” Yancopoulos said in a company release at the time. “We are honored to be in the position to be the first company to ever offer such a gene therapy advance for free to those in the U.S. and serves to highlight our belief that the biopharmaceutical industry can be a genuine force for good in the world.”

Giving out a gene therapy for free is “not a choice you can make financially if you’re not in a place like we are,” Chan acknowledged, pointing to products that have been “incredibly commercially successful over time.”

Through its nearly 40-year history, Regeneron has made a name for itself through blockbuster, wide-reaching products such as Bayer-partnered eye injection Eylea and inflammatory disease med Dupixent, a collaboration with Sanofi. As for the rest of the company’s drug portfolio, it doesn’t specifically chase drug areas that it thinks will have “huge commercial opportunity.”

Instead, “we follow the science,” Chan said, “and we mean that.”

Despite a market cap that puts it on par with many industry heavyweights, Regeneron considers itself something of a “scrappy start-up.” It’s a mindset that was ingrained in the company since its early biotech beginnings, but now, “we have more experience, we have more resources,” Chan said.

Outside of meeting its audience in “different places, in which they would have entry into getting to know us,” Chan emphasizes taking advantage of opportunities to do so.

“Things happen when you’re nimble,” she said, “when you’re already ready to help those new people who are just being introduced to you, to know who you are and to already have that ability to see who you are and how you operate.”

And how is it that the company operates?

“Doing well by doing good,” Chan said, a quote that comes from Schleifer’s father and now anchors Regeneron’s core values.
